Why Are They Called Cell Phones?

Questions 51-60
Read the passage. Choose the closest meaning of each underlined word in its context.

The word cellular describes the way a mobile network is organized. Instead of treating a whole region as one radio service area, engineers divide coverage into smaller areas called cells. Base-station antennas transmit and receive radio signals for these areas. The name refers to this arrangement of cells, not to a biological cell inside the handset or simply to the existence of towers. Antennas can be installed on buildings as well as towers.

The cellular approach helps increase network capacity: the amount of communication the system can handle. Radio resources are limited, so networks must utilize them efficiently. Frequencies can be used again in different places, with careful planning and control of interference, the unwanted effect of competing signals. This reuse allows more people to communicate than would otherwise be possible with the same radio resources.

Cells do not have to be uniform in size or shape. Their coverage can vary with antenna settings, buildings, terrain and other conditions. The neat hexagons in diagrams are a model, not the exact boundaries of real radio signals. Coverage areas can overlap; a phone may receive signals from more than one cell.

As a user moves, the network can coordinate a change to another suitable cell. This transfer is called a handover, or handoff. The network aims to keep the service working during the change. Cell sites are also connected to the wider network, which carries calls and data onward. Thus, a cell phone is named for the cellular network it uses, not for the route between two particular towers.

One Word, Several Meanings: Cell

Questions 61-70
Read the passage. Choose the closest meaning of each underlined word in its context.

An English word does not always have one fixed meaning. Consider cell. In a prison, a cell is a small room in which a prisoner is kept. In biology, a cell is a basic structural and functional unit of life. These two uses do not describe the same kind of object, although each suggests a separate unit or bounded space.

In an electrical device, an electrochemical cell produces electrical energy through chemical reactions. A battery can contain one or more such units. In a spreadsheet, a cell is one box where a user can enter data or a formula. Its position is identified by the intersection of a row and a column: in the usual letter-and-number notation, B3 is in column B, row 3.

These meanings are analogous in one respect: each identifies a unit within a larger arrangement. However, this comparison should not hide their differences. A living cell has biological processes; a spreadsheet box does not. The function of an electrical cell also differs from the purpose of a room in a prison.

Readers therefore need to interpret the word in context. Nearby words such as microscope, guard, voltage or formula provide clues. A precise interpretation depends on those clues, rather than on automatically choosing the first dictionary definition that comes to mind.

Perception and the Evidence We Notice

Questions 71-80
Read the passage. Choose the closest meaning of each underlined word in its context.

Perception involves more than receiving signals through the senses. A person must also select information and decide what it means. This process can be selective: a reader concentrating on a difficult paragraph may give little attention to a conversation nearby. The example concerns attention, not a claim that the reader has damaged hearing.

Imagine a classroom demonstration. Two listeners try to identify a faint tone among other sounds. Their prior experience may shape what they expect to hear. One listener reports a tone whenever the evidence is uncertain. The other waits for a clearer signal. The first listener may report more real tones, but may also report tones that were never played. A count of correct detections alone would not be a valid measure of which listener hears better.

To distinguish sensory ability from willingness to say yes, the class must consider both kinds of response. It should contrast successful detections with false alarms. This comparison reveals a possible response bias, or systematic tendency to favor one answer, rather than simply treating every confident reply as proof.

The demonstration illustrates why careful explanations must specify what was measured. A result may support a tentative conclusion without settling every question. An appropriate research philosophy is to compare explanations with evidence and revise an interpretation when better evidence becomes available.

What a Space Rock Can Tell Us

Questions 81-90
Read the passage. Choose the closest meaning of each underlined word in its context.

Meteorites are fragments of material from space that survive the journey through the atmosphere and reach the ground. Many come from asteroids. Their composition can help researchers investigate their origin. A useful comparison considers the minerals in a sample alongside other evidence; outward resemblance alone is not enough.

A meteorite can undergo changes after reaching Earth. Moisture and other conditions can alter its surface, producing weathering that damages some clues to its earlier history. Researchers therefore try to preserve samples carefully. The location and circumstances of a discovery are also relevant, because they help explain what may have happened to the specimen.

Now consider a hypothetical collection. If one kind of fragment is easier to recognize, that kind may be found more often. A collection dominated by it would not necessarily be representative of all the material that originally arrived. It would be misleading to infer original proportions simply from the number of objects on display.

Researchers must make any inference with these limits in mind. They can test an interpretation against chemical measurements and subsequent observations. An incomplete specimen can still provide valuable evidence, but a strong explanation considers what the evidence does not show as carefully as what it does.

Reading a Journey Through Different Eyes

Questions 91-100
Read the passage. Choose the closest meaning of each underlined word in its context.

Consider a historian who plans to undertake a study of an old journey. Two travelers left accounts of the same route, but one describes business arrangements while the other records daily life. Each account offers a unique contribution: something not provided in quite the same way by the other. Neither should automatically be treated as a complete record.

The travelers may describe the same vehicle differently. A passenger interested in comfort might discuss the seats, while a merchant concentrates on the space for goods. Their purposes help explain which features receive emphasis. A historian should not presume that every difference is an error; people can notice different details without inventing them.

However, a sensible explanation is not automatically a reliable one. Dates, maps and other records should be used to check the accounts. A preliminary comparison can reveal questions that deserve further investigation. If a writer could not predict a later event, a detailed description of that event may suggest that the account was revised afterward. This is a possible clue, not proof by itself.

The historian then examines a larger range of sources. Each has strengths and limitations, and a cautious revision of the first interpretation may be needed. Understanding a journey requires more than selecting the most entertaining story: it requires asking who wrote each account, for whom, when, and for what purpose.

Part 3 - Read an Academic Passage

Questions 11-20
Read the passage and choose one answer for each question. Paragraph numbers are provided for reference.

Perception: More Than a Clear Signal

1A person searching a crowded station for a friend may look directly at a notice without remembering it. The notice has not necessarily failed to reach the eyes; rather, the person is occupied with another task. Such everyday experiences reveal an important distinction between receiving sensory information and becoming aware of it. Perception is not a complete recording of the environment. It involves selecting information and interpreting what that information might mean.

2Attention helps make this selection manageable. At any moment, the senses provide more information than a person can examine closely. Focusing on a particular goal gives some information priority, while other information receives less processing. This limitation can extend across senses: concentrating on a demanding visual task can make an otherwise noticeable sound easier to miss. It would therefore be misleading to interpret every missed sound as evidence that the ears are damaged. The listener's current activity also matters.

3Expectations introduce another influence. Previous experience helps people anticipate what they are likely to encounter. A familiar word may be recognized even when a speaker's voice is partly covered by noise. In that situation, context makes incomplete information useful. However, the same process can produce errors. Someone expecting a delivery may interpret an unrelated sound as the doorbell. Expectations can improve an interpretation when they fit the evidence, but they can also encourage an interpretation that the evidence does not adequately support.

4To investigate such judgments, imagine an experiment in which listeners report whether a faint tone occurred during each trial. Some trials contain a tone, and others contain only background noise. A listener who frequently answers "yes" may detect many real tones, but may also report tones that were absent. Another listener may be more cautious and produce fewer false alarms while missing more actual tones. Counting correct detections alone would not provide an adequate comparison. Researchers must also consider the false alarms and the person's willingness to report an uncertain signal. This example illustrates a decision problem; it does not describe a particular published experiment.

5These distinctions have practical implications for warning systems. Simply making a warning louder may help, but does not guarantee that an occupied person will notice or correctly interpret it. Designers need to consider the activity being performed and whether different alerts can be distinguished. An effective warning should attract attention without creating so many unnecessary interruptions that people begin to disregard it. Understanding perception therefore requires both the physical signal and the person receiving it to be considered.

Part 4 - Read an Academic Passage

Questions 21-30
Read the passage and choose one answer for each question. Paragraph numbers are provided for reference.

Reconstructing an Asteroid from Its Fragments

1A meteorite displayed in a museum looks like an individual object, yet its scientific value often depends on connections to other samples. Many meteorites are fragments of larger bodies that once existed in space. By comparing their materials, scientists can investigate the histories of those parent bodies. The question is not simply what a rock contains, but what processes could have produced that particular combination of minerals and metals.

2One important distinction concerns heating. Some small bodies never melted throughout, so their fragments preserve mixtures of early solar-system materials. Others became hot enough for substantial melting and separation to occur. In such a differentiated body, dense metal could sink toward the center, while rocky materials formed outer layers. Later collisions could break the body apart. Consequently, a fragment consisting mainly of iron might sample an ancient interior, whereas a rocky fragment might represent a different layer of the same original body.

3Appearance alone, however, cannot reliably establish that two samples share an origin. Similar materials may develop in different places, and related fragments may look very different after experiencing different conditions. Scientists therefore compare several kinds of evidence, including mineral composition and chemical patterns. Matching patterns can strengthen the hypothesis of a shared source. A convincing explanation must also account for differences between the samples rather than selecting only their similarities.

4The journey to Earth adds a further complication. Atmospheric entry can melt a thin outer surface, producing a dark fusion crust without melting the entire interior. After landing, exposure to terrestrial water and air may alter the sample again. Researchers therefore distinguish changes that happened in space from changes acquired on Earth. Fresh interior material can provide evidence that a weathered surface no longer preserves. Careful handling and a record of where a specimen was found help researchers evaluate how reliable that evidence is.

5Finally, meteorite collections are not necessarily a balanced sample of everything in space. Some fragments survive atmospheric entry and weathering more successfully than others. Certain types are also easier to recognize on the ground. An abundant type in a museum collection therefore need not have been equally abundant in the original population of parent bodies. Combining laboratory evidence with observations of asteroids helps scientists address this limitation. Each sample supplies a partial record; reconstructing the larger history requires several independent clues to be considered together.

Task 3 - Academic Discussion

10 Minutes
You have 10 minutes. Write at least 100 words. Support your position with reasons and an example.
Professor Chen:

Universities have a finite budget for helping students improve their writing. Some want to invest more in AI systems that provide immediate feedback. Others prefer to fund additional small-group sessions with teachers. Which investment should receive priority, and why?

Amira:

I would prioritize AI feedback. It can highlight problems whenever a student is studying, not only during office hours. Teachers could then use class time to address more complex questions.

Leo:

I would fund more teacher-led sessions. A teacher can ask what a student intended to say and help the student evaluate an argument. Automated comments may be accurate about grammar but less useful about the quality of ideas.

Contribute your own view to the discussion. Develop a clear position with reasons and an example. You may acknowledge another perspective, but do not simply repeat the students' comments. Use linking words to connect your ideas.
